WordPress Plugin Review Checker

Scans your plugin's readme.txt and PHP source for the patterns behind common wordpress.org Plugin Directory review rejections: a Stable tag that doesn't match your plugin header's Version, missing required readme/header fields, a $_GET/$_POST/$_REQUEST/$_COOKIE/$_SERVER value echoed with no escaping function, and $_POST handling with no nonce check anywhere in the file. Everything runs in this tab; nothing is uploaded. A command-line version for CI is in the same repository (node check.mjs .).


Open your plugin's folder and select every .php file plus readme.txt (select-all works). Not at your project right now? instead.

No files selected yet.

Common questions

Why does a Stable tag / Version mismatch matter for WordPress plugin review?

The Plugin Directory serves whichever version readme.txt's Stable tag names, not whatever you most recently committed or tagged. If Stable tag still says an old version, users downloading or auto-updating your plugin get that old build even after you've shipped a new one -- and reviewers flag the mismatch on submission. This tool reads both files and tells you if they disagree.

What counts as "unescaped output" in a WordPress plugin?

Printing a value from $_GET, $_POST, $_REQUEST, $_COOKIE, or $_SERVER with echo/print/printf and no escaping function (esc_html, esc_attr, esc_url, sanitize_text_field, absint, and similar) wrapped around it. WordPress's own plugin-review guidance treats unescaped output as a security issue regardless of whether the specific input happens to be exploitable today -- the fix is standard, and reviewers ask for it as a matter of course.

Why does processing $_POST need a nonce check?

Without a nonce (check_admin_referer, check_ajax_referer, or wp_verify_nonce), a form handler can't tell a request submitted by your own plugin's form from one a malicious site tricked a logged-in user's browser into sending (cross-site request forgery). Plugin review looks for a nonce check anywhere in a file that processes $_POST; this tool does the same file-level check.

Is my plugin's source code uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser tool reads the files you select using the File API and never sends them anywhere -- everything happens in memory in your tab. The CLI never makes a network call either.

Does a clean report mean my plugin will pass wordpress.org Plugin Review?

No. This is evidence from pattern-matching your readme.txt, plugin header, and PHP source against known field names and function calls -- it is not the review process, and it is a line-level heuristic, not data-flow analysis. It can miss an escaping function applied a few lines away from the echo, a nonce check that exists but never actually runs before the $_POST read it's meant to guard, or a field spelled non-standardly. Always re-check against the Plugin Directory's own current guidelines before submitting.

More on the most common of these: Fixing a readme.txt "Stable tag" mismatch. Already run wordpress.org's own Plugin Check? See how it compares to this checker. Just reading the guidelines and checking your own files by eye? See what that read-through is most likely to miss.

Evidence, not a determination. This tool reports what pattern-matching found in the files you selected -- known readme.txt/plugin-header field names, and known WordPress escaping and nonce function calls. It is a line-level and file-level heuristic, not data-flow analysis: it cannot confirm an escaping function actually applies to the value printed, or that a nonce check it found actually runs before the $_POST read it's meant to guard. A clean report is not a guarantee wordpress.org Plugin Review will pass -- verify against the Plugin Directory's current guidelines before you submit.

stable-tag-mismatch.html.text:
Fixing a readme.txt "Stable tag" mismatch

A Stable tag mismatch is one of the most common notes a WordPress plugin gets during Plugin Directory review, and one of the easiest to introduce by accident: your readme.txt and your plugin's main file each carry their own version string, in two different files, in two different formats, and nothing forces them to move together.

Why it happens

The Plugin Directory serves whichever version readme.txt's Stable tag line names -- not your latest commit, not your latest tag, and not whatever the plugin header says. Bump the version in your main plugin file and forget the matching line in readme.txt (or the reverse) and the two drift apart. Users downloading or auto-updating your plugin keep getting the old build even after you've shipped the new one.

What "correct" looks like

FileLineWhat it controls
readme.txtStable tag: 1.4.2Which tagged version the directory actually serves to users
Main plugin file (PHP header comment)Version: 1.4.2What WordPress core shows in the Plugins screen and uses to detect an available update

The two values should read identically at every release -- or Stable tag may deliberately read trunk, which tells the directory to always serve whatever is in the SVN trunk rather than a tagged release. That's a valid, if less common, choice; it just isn't a version to compare against.

Find it automatically

The checker on this site reads both files and tells you immediately if they disagree, along with the other checks it runs (required readme/header fields, unescaped superglobal output, missing nonce checks on $_POST handlers). It runs as a browser tool (nothing uploaded) or a Node CLI you can add to your own pre-submission or pre-release check.

This is evidence of what the two files currently say, not a determination that Plugin Review will pass in every respect -- see the checker and its disclaimer for what else it can and can't see, and verify against the Plugin Directory's current guidelines before you submit or tag a release.

vs-manually-checking-against-the-guideli.text:
← WordPress Plugin Review Checker

This checker vs. manually checking against the guidelines yourself

Reading wordpress.org's Detailed Plugin Guidelines and re-checking your own readme.txt and PHP files against it by eye is the default first pass -- and every plugin author already does it. It reliably misses the two checks that require cross-referencing two separate files or scanning an entire file for the absence of something, which is exactly what this free tool automates.

What a manual guidelines read-through involves

wordpress.org publishes the Detailed Plugin Guidelines as prose -- readme.txt format, required and recommended header fields, security expectations, and more, laid out as paragraphs rather than a literal checklist. Preparing a submission means reading through that page, then re-reading your own readme.txt and every PHP file against it, holding each rule in mind as you go.

That works well for anything visible in one place: an obviously missing License line, a readme.txt that clearly does not follow the standard format. It works less well for a rule that spans two files that live nowhere near each other, or a rule that asks you to confirm an absence across every line of every file -- both are easy to satisfy in your head ("I checked the readme, I checked the header, both look fine") without ever performing the specific cross-check the rule actually requires.

The two checks a read-through is most likely to skip.
What the guidelines askReading through by eyeThis checker
readme.txt's Stable tag matches the plugin header's Version.Requires opening two files and comparing two short strings against each other -- easy to skip when each file individually looks correctly formatted.Reads both files and compares the two values automatically, every time.
Every $_POST handler is guarded by a nonce check somewhere in the same file.Requires holding the question open while scanning every line of every file -- tedious in a small plugin, easy to lose track of in a large one.Scans every file's $_POST usage against every known nonce-check function name.
Every superglobal value printed with echo/print/printf is escaped on the same line.An escaping function a few lines away, or on a different variable on the same line, can look right at a glance.Checks the exact line for both the output statement and an escaping call together.
Required readme.txt and header fields are all present.A field that "looks like it's probably there" from memory of past submissions.Checks each required field name explicitly and lists exactly which are missing.

Reading the guidelines is not wrong -- it is the only way to learn what a submission needs to look like at all, and this tool does not decide anything about your plugin the guidelines don't already say. What it automates is the narrow, mechanical cross-checking a careful read-through is most likely to let through under a deadline.

Run the free plugin review checker

The same 15-line example a guidelines read-through would pass

This is this tool's own bundled worked example -- short enough to read end to end in a few seconds: 

=== Example Plugin ===
Stable tag: 1.2.0
License: GPLv2 or later
License URI: https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-2.0.html

<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Example Plugin
 * Version: 1.3.0
 */
if ( isset( $_GET['name'] ) ) {
    echo 'Hello, ' . $_GET['name'];
}
function example_save_settings() {
    if ( isset( $_POST['example_option'] ) ) {
        update_option( 'example_option', $_POST['example_option'] );
    }
}

Read start to finish, both files look ordinary: the readme has every required field, the plugin header has a name and a version, and the code is short enough that nothing about it looks alarming. Run this checker's own detection logic against it and it reports three separate issues: the readme's Stable tag: 1.2.0 does not match the header's Version: 1.3.0; the echo on line 11 prints $_GET['name'] with no escaping function; and example_save_settings() reads $_POST['example_option'] with no check_admin_referer, check_ajax_referer, or wp_verify_nonce call anywhere in the file. All required readme and header fields are present, so none of the three issues is a missing-field problem a quick skim would catch -- each one needs the specific cross-check above.

Common questions

Isn't reading the guidelines and checking my own code enough?

It is the step every plugin author already takes, and it works for anything you can see in one place -- a missing License field, an obviously unescaped block. It works less well for anything that requires cross-referencing two files that live far apart (readme.txt's Stable tag against the main plugin file's Version header) or holding one rule in your head while scanning every line of every file in the plugin (does every $_POST read have a nonce check somewhere in this file?). Neither task is hard once you know to do it -- they are just easy to skip while reading for the dozens of other things the guidelines also cover.

How easy is it really to miss a Stable tag mismatch by eye?

In a 15-line worked example built specifically to demonstrate this tool -- short enough to read in ten seconds -- the readme.txt says Stable tag: 1.2.0 and the plugin file's header comment says Version: 1.3.0, three lines apart in two different files. A guidelines read-through checks each file looks correctly formatted; it does not by default diff the two version strings against each other, because nothing about reading either file in isolation calls attention to the other one.

Why is a missing nonce check easy to miss in a manual read?

Because the guidelines ask you to confirm a negative across an unbounded search: does any $_POST handler, anywhere in this file, lack a nonce check anywhere else in the same file? In a plugin with a handful of files that is tedious but doable. In a plugin with dozens of files handling forms, AJAX actions, and admin-post hooks, holding that question open while reading line by line is exactly the kind of check a deadline compresses first -- and unlike a formatting typo, a missing nonce check produces no visual cue that draws the eye.

Does this tool replace reading the guidelines?

No, and it checks only four specific, common patterns out of everything the Detailed Plugin Guidelines cover. Reading the guidelines is still how you learn what a first submission needs to look like at all. This tool exists for the narrower, mechanical part of that job -- cross-referencing two files and scanning every line for one of four patterns -- which is exactly the part a careful, unaided read-through is most likely to let through.

Already run wordpress.org's own Plugin Check? See how it compares to this checker. More on the most common single issue: Fixing a readme.txt "Stable tag" mismatch.

Evidence, not a determination. This tool reports what pattern-matching found in the files you selected -- known readme.txt/plugin-header field names, and known WordPress escaping and nonce function calls. It is a line-level and file-level heuristic, not data-flow analysis, and a clean report is not a guarantee wordpress.org Plugin Review will pass -- verify against the Plugin Directory's current guidelines before you submit.

vs-plugin-check.html.text:
← WordPress Plugin Review Checker

WordPress Plugin Review Checker vs. Plugin Check

A shared goal, at very different depth and setup cost. Plugin Check is wordpress.org's own official plugin: install it into a real or virtual WordPress site and it runs a broad battery of automated checks. This page checks four specific, common review-rejection patterns directly from your readme.txt and PHP source -- free, with no WordPress install, no PHP runtime, and no upload.

What each tool is for

Plugin Check (wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-check/) is an official plugin published by the WordPress Plugin Review Team. You install and activate it on an actual WordPress site -- a live one, or a local environment such as wp-env -- and then run it from its Tools admin screen or via wp plugin check <plugin> on WP-CLI. Once running, it checks broadly: coding-standards sniffs, security patterns (including escaping and nonce/CSRF issues), performance, accessibility, and internationalization, aiming to surface many of the same automated issues the plugin review process looks for before you submit.

This checker does the narrower version of one part of that job: you paste or select your plugin's readme.txt and PHP source, and it reports four specific, common review-rejection patterns -- a Stable tag/Version mismatch, missing required readme/header fields, a superglobal value echoed with no escaping function, and a $_POST handler with no nonce check anywhere in the file. It runs entirely in your browser or as a zero-dependency Node CLI, needs no WordPress install, no PHP runtime, and no database, and makes no network call of its own -- so it works on a plugin's files before they have ever been placed into a WordPress environment at all.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I want the broad, official, in-environment pass -- coding standards, accessibility, performance and i18n, not just these four patterns.Plugin Check -- that is its job, and this tool does not attempt the rest of it.
My plugin's files are not in a WordPress install yet -- a git checkout, an unzipped download, a folder I have not activated anywhere.This checker -- it reads the files directly and needs no WordPress site, real or local, to run against.
I just want to know if Stable tag matches Version, or catch an unescaped echo or a missing nonce check, right now, with nothing to install.This checker -- a fast, narrow answer to exactly those four questions.
I want the official pre-submission gate the review team's own tooling is built around.Plugin Check -- install it and run it before you submit or update.
I want this wired into my own CI with no PHP/WordPress runtime in the pipeline.This checker's node check.mjs . -- zero dependencies, reads local files only.

The two are complementary, not competing: install Plugin Check for the broad, official, in-environment pass, and reach for this tool the moment the question is only these four specific patterns on files that are not (yet) sitting inside a WordPress install.

Run the free plugin review checker

Common questions

Should I use this checker or wordpress.org's own Plugin Check?

They cover an overlapping goal at different depth and setup cost. Plugin Check (the wordpress.org Plugin Review Team's own official plugin, published at wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-check/) is a broad, comprehensive gate: once installed and activated on a real or virtual WordPress site, it runs a wide battery of automated checks -- coding-standards, security patterns including escaping and nonce/CSRF issues, performance, accessibility, and internationalization -- through its wp-admin screen or wp plugin check on WP-CLI. This page checks four specific, narrow patterns straight from your readme.txt and PHP source -- a Stable tag/Version mismatch, missing required readme/header fields, unescaped superglobal output, and a $_POST handler with no nonce check -- with no WordPress install, no PHP runtime, and no database, because it never talks to WordPress at all. If you want the broad, official, in-environment gate, run Plugin Check. If you want a fast answer to these four specific questions on files sitting on your machine right now, with nothing to install, this is the narrower tool for that.

Does Plugin Check already do everything this tool does?

For the four patterns this tool checks, yes, Plugin Check's broader battery covers similar ground -- readme/header field validation and security-pattern sniffs are part of what it runs. The difference is where and how you get the answer. Plugin Check needs an actual WordPress environment (a real site or a local one such as wp-env) with the plugin installed and activated before it can run at all, then reports through wp-admin or WP-CLI. This tool needs only the readme.txt and PHP files themselves -- a git checkout, an unzipped download, a folder that has never been near a WordPress install -- opened in a browser tab or passed to a Node CLI, with no setup step in between.

Why would I need a WordPress-free checker if Plugin Check already exists?

Three reasons this tool exists alongside it. First, Plugin Check has to run inside WordPress -- you install it as a plugin and either open its admin screen or run it through WP-CLI against a live or local site -- so it cannot check a plugin's files before they are placed into a WordPress environment at all; this tool reads the files directly, wherever they sit. Second, Plugin Check's battery is broad by design (coding standards, performance, accessibility and i18n alongside security and repo requirements), which is exactly right for a full pre-submission pass but slower to reach for when the question is only one of these four specific, high-frequency rejection causes. Third, this tool's browser page uploads nothing and its CLI makes no network call, so it works the same on a private plugin you have not pushed anywhere as on one already live in the directory.
